sections.markdown:
## C — Driving conditions part one: the SIPDE system, the three-second rule and stopping distance, night driving and headlight use, entering, driving and leaving freeways, bus shoulders and HOV lanes, diverging diamonds, freeway stops and emergencies, crashes, distraction, illegal behaviors, aggressive drivers, projecting loads and trailers
Knowledge domain: how a Minnesota driver scans for and handles hazards, keeps a safe following distance, drives at night, enters, uses and leaves freeways, handles freeway stops and emergencies, avoids distraction and illegal behaviors, and carries loads or tows trailers safely.

FACT_ID: sec11-F01 | anchor: A01
SIPDE is a five-step driving strategy: Scan, Identify, Predict, Decide and Execute. [A01]
Why it matters: the SIPDE steps in order are a likely test item.
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec11-F02 | anchor: A01
In the Scan step you search ahead, to the sides and behind for hazards before they arise, and look for escape routes near intersections, shopping areas, schools and commercial zones. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec11-F03 | anchor: A01
In the Identify step you locate hazards: moving vehicles and pedestrians, children and animals that can make short, fast moves, and fixed objects such as potholes, guard rails and trees that shape your driving plan. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec11-F04 | anchor: A01
In the Predict step you weigh the speed, distance and direction of each hazard, and cars moving into your path matter more than ones moving away or standing still. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec11-F05 | anchor: A01
In the Execute step you carry out your decision by signaling your presence with lights, horn or both, and by adjusting your speed, position or direction. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec11-F06 | anchor: A02
For the three-second rule, pick a fixed roadside point, start counting when the vehicle ahead passes it, and if you reach the point before counting three seconds you are following too closely. [A02]
Why it matters: the three-second rule is a core following distance item.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F07 | anchor: A02
The three-second rule assumes a standard-length vehicle in ideal conditions; in poor road conditions or in a longer vehicle, increase the count to four or five seconds. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F08 | anchor: A02
When someone tailgates you, ease off your speed a little and let that driver go around. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F09 | anchor: A02
It takes about 3/4 of a second to go from noticing danger to putting on the brakes, and stopping distance also depends on weather, tire tread and brake condition. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F10 | anchor: A02
Even though traffic is usually lighter at night, nearly half of all fatal traffic crashes in Minnesota happen after dark. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F11 | anchor: A02
Switch to low beam whenever an oncoming vehicle is within 1,000 feet, and whenever you are 200 feet or less behind another vehicle. [A02]
Why it matters: the two low beam distances are classic numeric items.
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F12 | anchor: A02
You should be able to stop within the stretch of road your headlights light up, which for most vehicles is no more than 350 feet on high beam. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F13 | anchor: A02
If oncoming headlights blind you, use the white edge line of the road as your guide, and for glare from behind, use a day-night mirror or adjust your mirror. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec11-F14 | anchor: A03
At the end of most freeway entry ramps an acceleration lane lets you build speed to match the traffic you are joining. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F15 | anchor: A03
When merging onto a freeway you must yield to vehicles already on it, signal, and move into a safe gap in the nearest lane. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F16 | anchor: A03
Do not stop on an entry ramp or in the acceleration lane unless it is absolutely necessary. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F17 | anchor: A03
Where there is no acceleration lane and the entry ramp has a Yield sign, obey it, stop if necessary, and never force your way into traffic. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F18 | anchor: A03
Freeway ramp meters sit about halfway down the entry ramp, usually operate at peak travel hours, and it is illegal to drive through their red light. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F19 | anchor: A03
On the freeway keep close to the speed of surrounding traffic without ever exceeding the posted limit, and stay in the right-hand lane if you are slower than others. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec11-F20 | anchor: A04
Transit and metro mobility buses may drive on a freeway or expressway shoulder only when main-line traffic is under 35 mph, never more than 15 mph faster than that traffic and never above 35 mph. [A04]
Why it matters: the bus shoulder limits are easy to confuse with lane splitting limits.
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec11-F21 | anchor: A04
Freeway message signs warn of crashes, stalled vehicles and other conditions ahead, and during an AMBER Alert they may describe a vehicle so drivers who spot it can tell law enforcement. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec11-F22 | anchor: A04
High-occupancy vehicle lanes are only for motorcycles, buses and vehicles carrying two or more people. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec11-F23 | anchor: A05
In a diverging diamond interchange the lanes cross over at each end of the bridge, so instead of turning sharply left across opposing traffic you veer left to reach the ramp. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F24 | anchor: A05
Diverging diamond interchanges can cut overall traffic delays by up to 60 percent and have fewer, more spread-out conflict points and shorter pedestrian crossings. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F25 | anchor: A05
Stopping or parking on an interstate freeway is illegal except in an emergency, and running out of fuel does not count as one, so it can bring a citation. [A05]
Why it matters: running out of fuel is a classic trick item.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F26 | anchor: A05
In a freeway emergency, park on the shoulder as far from traffic as you can, signal for help by lifting the hood and opening the trunk or by tying a white cloth to the antenna or a door handle, and use hazard lights. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F27 | anchor: A05
Place any flares or reflectors from 100 to 500 feet behind your vehicle along the right edge of the main road. [A05]
Why it matters: the flare placement range is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F28 | anchor: A05
Stay with your vehicle if possible, because walking in the part of the highway used by traffic is illegal and extremely dangerous. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F29 | anchor: A05
Backing up or turning around on a freeway is illegal except for emergency and road repair vehicles doing their jobs. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F30 | anchor: A05
When an emergency vehicle with lights and siren comes up behind you on the freeway, signal, move to the nearest side and stop without slamming the brakes or swerving, and watch for more before pulling out. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F31 | anchor: A05
Stay at least 500 feet behind any firefighting vehicle. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec11-F32 | anchor: A06
If you miss your freeway exit, go on to the next one, and never back up or make a U-turn to get back. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec11-F33 | anchor: A06
You can add caretaker information to your DVS record so that, after a crash, officers know someone at home depends on you. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec11-F34 | anchor: A06
After a crash with injuries stay where you are and, if able, call 911 or the nearest law enforcement agency, but after a property-damage-only crash move to a safe place before getting out. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec11-F35 | anchor: A06
Driver distraction is a leading factor in Minnesota crashes, accounting for at least 25 percent of all crashes each year. [A06]
Why it matters: the distraction share is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec11-F36 | anchor: A06
The three types of distraction are visual, taking your eyes off the road; mechanical or physical, taking your hands off the wheel; and cognitive, being lost in thought. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec11-F37 | anchor: A07
Texting, emailing or going online with a phone or wireless device while driving is illegal in Minnesota, including while stopped in traffic. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F38 | anchor: A07
A driver under 18 holding an instruction permit or provisional license may not use a cell phone at all, handheld or hands-free, except to call 911 in an emergency. [A07]
Why it matters: the under-eighteen phone ban is a likely test item.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F39 | anchor: A07
Wearing headphones or earphones in both ears at once to listen to a radio or other sound device while driving is illegal. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F40 | anchor: A07
Faced with an aggressive driver, never challenge them: keep clear, do not meet their eyes, and keep things from getting worse. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F41 | anchor: A07
Driving with a load or with more than three people in the front seat is illegal when it blocks your view or interferes with control. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F42 | anchor: A07
No load on a motor vehicle may extend more than three feet ahead of its front wheels or front bumper. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F43 | anchor: A07
A load extending four feet or more past the rear needs a red, yellow or orange flag at least 16 inches square at its end, and at night a red lantern or lamp visible from at least 500 feet. [A07]
Why it matters: the rear load flag rule is a likely numeric item.
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F44 | anchor: A07
On a passenger vehicle a load may not extend past the left fender line, or more than six inches past the right fender line. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec11-F45 | anchor: A07
When pulling a camper or trailer, keep at least 500 feet of following distance from other vehicles. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0082]

Misconceptions: running out of fuel is not an emergency that permits stopping on a freeway; a missed exit never justifies backing up; a hands-free phone is still banned for permit and provisional drivers under eighteen; a three-second gap is only the minimum for ideal conditions.
Mnemonics: Scan, Identify, Predict, Decide, Execute; dim within a thousand ahead or two hundred behind; three seconds ideal, four or five when it is bad or long; flares one to five hundred feet back; four feet out the back needs a flag.
Glossary: SIPDE means the five-step scan, identify, predict, decide and execute strategy; acceleration lane means the lane at the end of an entry ramp used to reach freeway speed; deceleration lane means the lane used to slow before an exit ramp; diverging diamond interchange means an interchange where traffic crosses to the left side on the bridge to avoid left turns across traffic; AMBER Alert means a statewide alert issued for a child abduction.
